title: Sexual Violence in the Bible
lead: The Bible tells several stories of rape and sexual coercion without softening them: Dinah (Genesis 34), the Levite's concubine (Judges 19), David and Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11) and Amnon and Tamar (2 Samuel 13). It condemns them as "a disgraceful thing in Israel," while its laws reflect an ancient world in which women's consent was rarely asked.

sections.b: The narratives share features: a woman's voice is barely heard, male relatives decide what happens, and revenge often brings wider violence (Genesis 34:25–29; Judges 20; 2 Samuel 13:28–29). The phrase "disgraceful thing" (nevalah) links Dinah's and Tamar's stories (Genesis 34:7; 2 Samuel 13:12). The laws (Exodus 22:16–17; Deuteronomy 22:23–29) punish the man, require payment and in some cases marriage, and protect a woman assaulted "in the open country," where no one could hear her cry. Modern readers, Jewish and Christian, have paid new attention to these texts, asking how to read them honestly (Phyllis Trible, Texts of Terror, 1984).
